title: The useState Hook
description: Learn how to add state to functional components using the useState hook.

data.text: **State** is data that changes over time in your application. The `useState` hook is the most fundamental React hook — it lets you add reactive state to functional components so the UI updates automatically when the data changes.
Call `useState` with an initial value. It returns an array with two elements: the current state value and a function to update it. By convention we destructure these into meaningful variable names.

data.title: useState Basics
data.content: Adding a counter to a component

data.text: Call `useState` as many times as you need. Each call manages an independent piece of state. Group related values into one object only if they always change together.

data.title: Multiple States

data.text: When storing an object in state, always create a new object when updating. React uses reference equality to detect changes, so mutating the existing object will not trigger a re-render.

data.title: Object State
Never Mutate State Directly
data.text: Direct mutation is invisible to React. Always create a new object or array when updating state.
When the new state depends on the previous state, pass a function to the setter. This guarantees you always work with the latest value, even if multiple updates happen in quick succession.

data.title: Functional Updates
data.content: Using a function form for safe state updates

data.text: If the initial state requires an expensive computation, pass a function to `useState`. React calls that function once during the initial render.

data.title: Lazy Initial State

terms.definition: Mutable data inside a component that triggers re-renders when changed.
The second value returned by useState; updates state and schedules a re-render.
Passing a function to the setter to compute new state from the previous state.
React calling the component function again to produce new UI.

data.caption: How useState manages state and triggers re-renders.
data.definition:
flowchart TB
    A[setState called] --> B[Schedule re-render]
    B --> C[Component function runs]
    C --> D[New JSX returned]
    D --> E[Virtual DOM diffed]
    E --> F[Real DOM updated]

data.title: Exercise: Build a Counter
data.description: Create a counter with increment, decrement, and reset buttons.
steps: Create a Counter component in src/components/Counter.jsx.
Add three buttons: Increment, Decrement, Reset.
Use functional updates for increment and decrement.
Use direct value update for reset.
data.expectedOutcome: A working counter that updates correctly and resets to zero.

items.question: Why is the setter function named setCount and not updateCount?
items.answer: Naming is a convention. `set` + capitalized state name (setCount, setUser) is the React community standard.

items.question: Can I use useState without importing it?
items.answer: No. Hooks must be imported from 'react'. React relies on call order, so do not conditionally call hooks.

items.question: Does calling setState immediately update the variable?
items.answer: No. State updates are asynchronous. React batches updates and applies them during the next render.

items.question: When should I use useReducer instead of useState?
items.answer: Use useReducer when state logic is complex, involves multiple sub-values, or when the next state depends on the previous state in a non-trivial way.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: useState adds reactive state to functional components.
Never mutate state directly; always create new values.
Use functional updates when new state depends on old state.
Lazy initialization avoids expensive work on every render.
data.takeaway: State powers dynamic, interactive UIs. Next, you will learn how user actions trigger state changes through events.
